tasks.short: Attend toolbox talks, read site safety rules, do a last-minute risk check, keep certificates current, and work safely.

steps.what: Operator attends toolbox meetings on site
Operator reads the site safety plan and project rules: in the site office binder today, on the phone after the change
Operator fills in a last-minute risk check before each job: on a paper card today, as a phone checklist after the change
Operator keeps machine certificates and safety courses current
Operator follows safety regulations while operating the machine

tasks.design: Site rules and the relevant parts of the safety plan open on the operator's phone in the contractor's site app ({OTHER}), with a read confirmation, and the last-minute risk check is a short phone checklist. Certificate expiry dates sit in the {LMS} with reminders; toolbox talks and safe operation stay as they are.
tasks.previous_blocker: Rules sat in binders at the site office and risk checks were paper cards.
tasks.enabler_now: Construction apps hold checklists and documents on phones.
tasks.still_hard: Safety is behaviour on the machine; a checklist ticked without thought adds nothing.
tasks.human_edge: Stopping when something feels wrong, even when the planning says go.

reach.task: Brief new operators on site rules
reach.learn: Whether read confirmations replace site office briefings.

evidence.claim: Construction software keeps site diaries, checklists and handover reports.
Logs per worker can observe presence and performance and need works council consent.

assumptions: Boundary: from toolbox talks to safe operation; incident investigation is outside.
Input contract: site rules and safety plan sections published by the site manager; certificate dates recorded by the employer's training coordinator; fallback is the site office binder.
Risk checks are kept per job, not used to judge operators.

Toolbox talks, the risk check and operation keep their full time; ticking a phone checklist is not faster than a card. s2 keeps 70 because the walk to the site office goes but the rules are still read. s4 keeps 50 because expiry dates and reminders come from the system; booking courses stays.
unknowns: Whether operators carry phones they can use on site.
research_questions: Do phone risk checks change what operators notice?

incremental.description: Site manager keeps site rules current in the app.
No ongoing focal upkeep: the site manager keeps the rules and the training coordinator the certificate dates; learning the app is a one-off.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Low: the operator stays on one site for months and reads the rules once, so little reading time changes (6.5); high: frequent site changes (9.5).

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

tasks.short: Agree signals with the driver, guide the machine's movement by hand or radio, and keep people out of the danger zone.

steps.what: Operator agrees hand signals and radio channel with the other driver
Operator signals operators to guide the movement of tractor-drawn machines
Operator keeps watch for people entering the danger zone

tasks.design: No change is proposed: signalling is live, in-person work where a person's eyes and voice are the safety measure. Machine cameras and proximity sensors can support the driver, but they do not replace the person giving signals.
tasks.previous_blocker: Nothing blocks it; this is physical guidance.
tasks.enabler_now: Not applicable; no digital step exists to improve.
tasks.still_hard: Everything: signals depend on line of sight, trust and split-second judgement.
tasks.human_edge: Seeing what the driver cannot and stopping the machine in time.

reach.task: Work with a banksman on lifts
reach.learn: Whether radio protocols could be shared across trades.

evidence.claim: Machine-mounted cameras and proximity sensors support drivers but do not replace a person giving signals.
Employers must control the risks of moving equipment under national working conditions rules.

assumptions: Boundary: the signalling itself during one movement.
Input contract: none; the lift or move plan comes from the site manager on paper or by talk.
No monitoring of the operator is added.
All steps stay as they are.
unknowns: How often the operator acts as signaller rather than driver.
research_questions: None for automation; safety research on signalling is a separate field.

incremental.description: No new work: the design adds no tool or record to this task.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Signalling is entirely physical, live work; nothing in it is paperwork.

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

tasks.short: Check cable and pipe maps before digging, watch the work area, stop for hazards, report near misses and do the daily machine check.

steps.what: Operator checks the printed cable and pipe map before digging
Operator monitors operations: people, slopes, cables and traffic
Operator stops work and phones the site manager when health and safety standards are not met
Operator writes near-miss reports: on paper forms today, in a phone form with photo after the change
Operator checks the near-miss report: what happened, where, and a photo that shows the situation
Operator sends the checked near-miss report to the site manager
Site manager follows up reported situations
Operator does the daily machine safety check: with a paper checklist today, with a phone checklist after the change
Operator checks any defect report before it goes: the machine, the defect, a photo and whether the machine may still run
Operator sends the checked defect report to the workshop

tasks.design: The cable and pipe map requested by the site manager shows on a tablet in the cab, overlaid on the machine's position, instead of a printout. Near misses go into a phone form with photo in the contractor's site app ({OTHER}), which the operator checks and sends to the site manager; the daily machine check is a phone checklist, and the operator checks any defect report and sends it to the workshop; watching and stopping work stay with the operator.
tasks.previous_blocker: Maps were printed and checked against landmarks, and reports were paper forms.
tasks.enabler_now: Construction apps hold checklists and defect logs on phones; cable and pipe maps are digital.
tasks.still_hard: Maps are not always accurate; only hand digging near cables is safe.
tasks.human_edge: Feeling the bucket touch something that should not be there and stopping.

reach.task: Track near misses across the project
reach.learn: Whether photo reports raise the number of near misses reported.

evidence.claim: Construction software logs defects and checklists and builds reports.
Before digging, the cable and pipe locations must be requested under national rules.
Location tracking of workers needs a legitimate interest and necessity.

assumptions: Boundary: from preparing to dig to reports followed up; repairs are outside.

Input contract: cable and pipe maps requested by the site manager for each dig zone; machine position from the machine's guidance system; checklist items set by the equipment manager; fallback is paper.
Machine position is used for the map only, not to track the operator.

Watching the area, stopping work, the machine check and both report checks keep their full time; ticking a phone checklist is not faster than paper. s1 keeps 60 because the map shows the machine's position but is still checked. s4 keeps 85 because the form sets the layout; the operator still writes what happened.
unknowns: Whether the machines have guidance screens or tablets.
How often near misses are reported now.
research_questions: Do cab maps reduce cable strikes?

incremental.description: Site manager loads maps for each dig zone.
No ongoing focal upkeep: the site manager loads the maps and the equipment manager sets the checklist; learning the forms is a one-off.

approvals.approved_version: The near-miss report with what happened, place and photo exactly as checked by the operator in s4c, sent once to the site manager in the site app; any change needs a new check.
The defect report with machine, defect, photo and run decision exactly as checked by the operator in s6c, sent once to the workshop queue in the site app; any change needs a new check.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Low: the machine has no guidance system, so the map cannot show its position and is matched to landmarks as today (3.8); high: guidance on the machine (8.0).

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

tasks.short: Choose the attachment, fetch it, fasten and lock it with the hitch, test the lock and log the change.

steps.what: Operator chooses the blade or bucket for the job
Operator fetches the attachment from the yard
Operator fastens bulldozer blades or other attachments using hitches
Operator checks the locking pin and tests the hold
Operator logs the attachment change: in the paper machine logbook today, in the equipment app after the change

tasks.design: The machine logbook moves to the contractor's equipment app ({OTHER}) on the phone, where the attachment change is logged; this takes as long as the paper line. Choosing, fitting and testing attachments stay fully manual.
tasks.previous_blocker: Nothing blocked it; this is mechanical work with a small paper log.
tasks.enabler_now: Construction apps plan equipment and hold logs on phones.
tasks.still_hard: Fitting and checking the lock is physical and safety-critical.
tasks.human_edge: Hearing and feeling that the lock has seated properly.

reach.learn: Whether app logs show which attachments wear fastest.

evidence.claim: Construction ERP apps plan staff and equipment and log hours in the app.
Logs per worker need works council consent; this log is per machine.

assumptions: Boundary: from choosing to logging the attachment; repairs are outside.
Input contract: machine and attachment list kept by the equipment manager in the app; fallback is the paper logbook.
The log is per machine, not per operator.
Choosing, fitting, testing and logging keep their full time; two taps are not faster than one short paper line.
unknowns: Whether the contractor has an equipment app.
research_questions: Does a per-machine log help plan attachment maintenance?

incremental.description: No upkeep: the equipment manager keeps the machine and attachment list, and learning the log is a one-off.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: No saving: choosing, fetching, fitting and testing are physical, and the log line takes as long in the app as on paper (0.0).

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

role.altitude: The equipment operator keeps every physical and safety task; checklists, maps and logs move to the phone and cab.
skills_to_grow: Using cab maps without trusting them blindly
role.ambitious_version: An operator with the right map in the cab and paperwork that takes minutes.

job.title: Operating Engineers and Other Construction Equipment Operators
